function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script).  
I’ve also included the exact file contents that should be added to the repository.

> **NOTE** – The `create_a_docker_file` helper only knows about Python images, so for a Node.js project we’ll hand‑craft the Dockerfile instead of calling that helper.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use the official lightweight Node.js image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "src/index.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small, fast, and contains the latest LTS Node.js release.  
> * Installing dependencies before copying the source allows Docker to cache the `npm ci` layer.  
> * The app is assumed to listen on port **3000** (adjust if your app uses a different port).

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s-deployment.yaml` at the root of the repo with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_DOCKERHUB_USERNAME>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your image
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys two replicas of the container.  
> * Exposes the app via a `ClusterIP` service on port 80, forwarding traffic to container port 3000.  
> * Replace `<YOUR_DOCKERHUB_USERNAME>` with your Docker Hub username (or any registry you’re using).

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout repository
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
      # Uncomment and configure if you want to deploy automatically
      # uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v3
      # with:
      #   manifests: k8s-deployment.yaml
      #   kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
```

> **How it works**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Builds the Docker image and pushes it to Docker Hub.  
> * Requires two secrets in the repo settings:  
>   * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username.  
>   * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (not your password).  
> * If you want automatic deployment to a cluster, uncomment the “Deploy to Kubernetes” step and add a `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` secret.

---

## 3️⃣ Add all changed files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s-deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, and GitHub Actions workflow"
git push origin main
```

---

### 🎉 Done!

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically build and publish the Docker image whenever you push to `main`.  
If you enabled the optional deployment step, it will also apply the Kubernetes manifests to your cluster.
